variants.title: Assemble the portfolio
variants.context: A benchmark portfolio starts from the release decision, not from a leaderboard. Write the behavior contract, map each claim to evidence, freeze the protocol, then apply the hard gates.
variants.prompt: A team is picking benchmarks for a grounded support assistant and starts by asking which public leaderboard to run. Put the portfolio steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the protocol by versioning data, prompts, retrieval state, tools, decoding settings, and aggregation rules.
Apply the hard gates by inspecting confidence intervals, critical slices, contamination, and regression limits.
Write the behavior contract by naming the user jobs, the languages that matter, and the failures that would block release.
Map each claim to evidence by pairing a benchmark with product cases, a scoring method, and a minimum slice size.

variants.hint: The first question is which decision the evidence must support.
variants.explanation: Scope comes before dataset choice, and the aggregate score is read last, after the gates.

variants.title: Assemble the portfolio
variants.context: A benchmark portfolio starts from the release decision, not from a leaderboard. Write the behavior contract, map each claim to evidence, freeze the protocol, then apply the hard gates.
variants.prompt: A multimodal assistant reports one blended score from a text-only suite and nobody can reproduce last week's run. Put the corrective steps in order.

items.text: Record the tokenizer, prompt template, image preprocessing, decoding settings, and answer extraction used for the run.
Add visual grounding, layout, and OCR-sensitivity cases beside the text set, each with its own slice floor.
Read the gate on the recorded run, treating any failed modality slice as a blocker rather than a footnote.
State that the product must read document layout and images, and that a modality-specific safety failure blocks release.

variants.hint: A blended score cannot be repaired at the gate if the contract never named the modality.
variants.explanation: Coverage gaps are contract failures. Naming the promised behavior first is what makes the missing slice visible.

variants.title: Assemble the portfolio
variants.context: A benchmark portfolio starts from the release decision, not from a leaderboard. Write the behavior contract, map each claim to evidence, freeze the protocol, then apply the hard gates.
variants.prompt: A code assistant team wants to claim that generated changes preserve existing behavior. Put the steps that turn that claim into release evidence in order.

items.text: Compare the result against the frozen baseline and check the regression limit before reporting any average.
Name the jobs the assistant performs on the repository and declare that a silent behavior change blocks release.
Pin the runtime image, dependency lockfile, test command, prompt template, and decoding settings for the run.
Pair repository test execution and a security regression set with a minimum case count for each protected area.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what counts as a failure at all?
variants.explanation: The claim decides the evidence, the frozen protocol makes the result reproducible, and the gate reads it last.

variants.title: Read the gate in order
variants.context: A defensible release gate is read in a fixed order: quarantine contaminated evidence, measure uncertainty, check protocol stability, protect critical slices, and only then request bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A candidate scores well, but a screen finds that 6 percent of the holdout has near-duplicates in the training corpus. Put the gate steps in order.

items.text: Check every critical slice against its own minimum instead of the portfolio average.
Request a monitored canary with abort thresholds and a rollback target.
Check protocol stability by comparing prompt variants and judge disagreement on the same cases.
Measure uncertainty on the remaining evidence and read the conservative regression, not the point estimate.
Quarantine the contaminated cases, because more samples cannot restore the holdout's independence.

variants.hint: Contaminated evidence is removed before anything is computed from it.
variants.explanation: Contamination invalidates evidence, so it is handled first; passing offline evidence earns only bounded exposure.

variants.title: Read the gate in order
variants.context: A defensible release gate is read in a fixed order: quarantine contaminated evidence, measure uncertainty, check protocol stability, protect critical slices, and only then request bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A candidate shows a 0.4 point gain, no contamination, and a judge that disagrees with itself across prompt variants. Put the gate steps in order.

items.text: Hold the rollout rather than requesting exposure on an unstable protocol.
Confirm the contamination screen is clean so the holdout still counts as independent evidence.
Verify that no critical slice fell below its floor while the aggregate stayed flat.
Calibrate or adjudicate the judge, because a score that moves with the prompt template is not a release signal.
Compute the confidence interval and note that the gain is smaller than the interval width.

variants.hint: A score that depends on incidental setup choices is not yet evidence.
variants.explanation: Large prompt variance or judge disagreement means the protocol, not the candidate, is being measured.

variants.title: Read the gate in order
variants.context: A defensible release gate is read in a fixed order: quarantine contaminated evidence, measure uncertainty, check protocol stability, protect critical slices, and only then request bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A candidate improves the portfolio average by 2 points while the minority-language slice drops below its declared minimum. Put the gate steps in order.

items.text: Record the blocker and the owner rather than requesting canary exposure.
Confirm the holdout is uncontaminated so the comparison is still valid.
Read the confidence interval on the aggregate delta before treating the 2 point gain as real.
Confirm the protocol was frozen and that both candidates ran the same prompts and extraction rules.
Block on the failed language slice, because a high average cannot cancel a failed critical subgroup.

variants.hint: Which check has its own minimum that the average is not allowed to override?
variants.explanation: A critical slice gets its own floor. Its failure is a blocker even when the portfolio average passes.

variants.title: Fund the critical evidence first
variants.context: Allocate the evaluation budget by decision value. A suite costs its case count multiplied by its cost per case, and every suite declared critical is funded before any optional suite is considered.
variants.prompt: A release plan declares two critical suites: 200 continuous-integration executable checks at 0.001 dollars per case, and a 600 case critical-slice review at 0.12 dollars per case. The budget is 150 dollars. How many dollars remain for optional suites?
variants.hint: Multiply cases by cost per case for each critical suite before subtracting from the budget.
variants.explanation: Critical evidence is funded first, so the remainder is the budget minus every declared critical suite.

mistakes.feedback: You dropped the 0.20 dollars for the executable checks; a cheap critical suite still spends budget.
That is the cost of the critical evidence, not what is left of the budget.

variants.title: Fund the critical evidence first
variants.context: Allocate the evaluation budget by decision value. A suite costs its case count multiplied by its cost per case, and every suite declared critical is funded before any optional suite is considered.
variants.prompt: The same two critical suites cost 72.20 dollars in total, and the budget is 100 dollars. Two optional suites are available: a 1000 case capability comparison at 0.02 dollars per case and a 150 case preference calibration at 0.35 dollars per case. The planner adds the cheapest optional suites that still fit. What is the total planned cost in dollars?
variants.hint: Work out what each optional suite costs, then check which of them the remaining budget can actually cover.
variants.explanation: Optional suites are added cheapest first and only while they fit, so an unaffordable suite is skipped rather than trimmed.

mistakes.feedback: You funded every suite; the 52.50 dollar calibration set does not fit the 27.80 dollars that remain.
You stopped at the critical evidence and skipped an optional suite the budget can afford.

variants.title: Fund the critical evidence first
variants.context: Allocate the evaluation budget by decision value. A suite costs its case count multiplied by its cost per case, and every suite declared critical is funded before any optional suite is considered.
variants.prompt: A team lists three suites: an 800 case executable regression set at 0.005 dollars per case marked critical, a 250 case critical-slice human review at 0.40 dollars per case marked critical, and a 200 case preference calibration at 0.30 dollars per case marked optional. How many dollars must the budget cover before any optional suite is considered?
variants.hint: Only the suites the team declared critical belong in this figure.
variants.explanation: The critical floor is the sum of the declared critical suites. A budget that cannot cover it is not a fundable plan.

mistakes.feedback: You included the preference calibration set, which the team marked optional.
You dropped the 4 dollars for the executable regression set.

variants.title: Match evidence to the claim
variants.context: A benchmark belongs in the portfolio because it supports a product claim. Capability benchmarks, product task sets, risk and reliability suites, and human review each answer a different question.
variants.prompt: A retrieval assistant must claim that its answers are supported by the documents it retrieved. It currently reports only a general knowledge benchmark score. What evidence closes the gap?
options: A larger sample of the same multidomain knowledge questions.
Citation precision and recall checks scored against the retrieved documents.
A broader public leaderboard covering more academic subjects.
optionFeedback: More cases narrow uncertainty on a question the product never asked.
Citation checks measure the promised behavior directly, against the sources actually retrieved.
Wider academic coverage still measures knowledge rather than grounding in retrieved text.
variants.hint: Which evidence looks at the retrieved documents themselves?
variants.explanation: A benchmark belongs in the portfolio because it supports a product claim. Grounding claims need citation evidence, not more knowledge questions.

variants.title: Match evidence to the claim
variants.context: A benchmark belongs in the portfolio because it supports a product claim. Capability benchmarks, product task sets, risk and reliability suites, and human review each answer a different question.
variants.prompt: The same assistant must also claim that it resists instructions hidden inside retrieved pages. Which evidence supports that claim?
options: A common-sense multiple-choice set run at a higher sample size.
A risk suite of retrieved passages carrying injected instructions and side-effect checks.
A larger human preference sample on normal customer questions.
optionFeedback: Constrained multiple-choice tasks cannot expose an injection that arrives through retrieval.
Adversarial retrieved text is the only evidence that exercises the failure being claimed.
Preference on normal traffic says nothing about behavior under hostile retrieved text.
variants.hint: Which suite targets harmful or irreversible failure modes on purpose?
variants.explanation: Risk and reliability suites exist to probe the failure boundary. Representative traffic rarely contains the attack.

variants.title: Match evidence to the claim
variants.context: A benchmark belongs in the portfolio because it supports a product claim. Capability benchmarks, product task sets, risk and reliability suites, and human review each answer a different question.
variants.prompt: A multimodal assistant reports one aggregate built entirely from text cases and the team calls the portfolio complete. What is the correct reading?
options: The aggregate is incomplete until visual grounding, layout, and OCR slices report separately.
The aggregate is complete because the text cases already cover the shared reasoning core.
The aggregate is complete once its sample size passes the declared slice floor.
optionFeedback: A text-only aggregate is incomplete evidence for a product that must read images and documents.
A shared reasoning core is an assumption, not measured evidence about image or layout handling.
Sample size narrows uncertainty on the tested dimension and adds no evidence about untested ones.
variants.hint: Ask which promised behaviors have no independent evidence at all.
variants.explanation: Evidence coverage asks whether each promised dimension has its own suitable evidence. It is not the same as a high score.

variants.title: Store the four identities
variants.context: Every stored result carries four identities: candidate identity describes what was run, test identity describes what it was run on, judgment identity describes how it was scored, and decision identity describes what the score was allowed to authorize.
variants.prompt: An engineer investigating a regression opens the stored result. Match each recorded field to the identity it belongs to.

pairs.label: Candidate identity
pairs.detail: Model, adapter, system prompt, decoding parameters, and the retrieval corpus snapshot.

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: Dataset split version, case IDs, slice labels, and the contamination screen result.

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: Metric version, rubric, judge model and prompt, and the adjudication policy.

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: Predeclared thresholds, baseline version, rollout owner, and rollback trigger.

variants.hint: Ask whether the field describes what ran, what it ran on, how it was scored, or what it authorized.
variants.explanation: Reproducing a score needs all four. A missing identity turns a regression investigation into guesswork.

variants.title: Store the four identities
variants.context: Every stored result carries four identities: candidate identity describes what was run, test identity describes what it was run on, judgment identity describes how it was scored, and decision identity describes what the score was allowed to authorize.
variants.prompt: Two runs disagree and nobody can say why. Match each missing field to the identity that should have carried it.

pairs.label: Candidate identity
pairs.detail: The tool version the assistant called during the run.

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: The prompt template and sampling policy applied to the cases.

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: The reviewer instructions given to the human raters.

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: The confidence method used to compare against the baseline.

variants.hint: Reviewer instructions belong with scoring, not with the cases themselves.
variants.explanation: Each identity answers one question. Splitting them keeps a scoring change from being mistaken for a candidate change.

variants.title: Store the four identities
variants.context: Every stored result carries four identities: candidate identity describes what was run, test identity describes what it was run on, judgment identity describes how it was scored, and decision identity describes what the score was allowed to authorize.
variants.prompt: A release review asks four questions about last night's run. Match each question to the identity that answers it.

pairs.label: Candidate identity
pairs.detail: Which decoding settings and index snapshot produced these outputs?

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: Which case IDs and split version were scored?

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: Which executable test image decided pass or fail?

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: Which approved exception let the rollout proceed?

variants.hint: An approved exception is part of what the score was allowed to authorize.
variants.explanation: Storing the identities separately lets a reviewer name the exact thing that changed between two results.
